Customer retention by industry: hospitality keeps 55%, media keeps 84%

Not every industry keeps its customers the same way. According to data compiled by CustomerGauge, NPS Benchmarks and MIT CISR, customer retention in 2018 ranged from 84% in media to 55% in hospitality, travel and restaurants. That is almost thirty points between the top and the bottom of the ranking.

This is more than a statistical curiosity. It says something precise about the relationship between a business and its customers, and above all about how much information those customers leave behind before they go.

A ranking that surprises

At the top of the table are media and professional services (84%), followed by automotive and transportation and insurance (83%). Next come IT services (81%), construction and engineering (80%), and financial services and telecommunications (78%).

At the bottom, three groups fall clearly behind: consumer services and manufacturing (67%), retail (63%) and, in last place, hospitality, travel and restaurants (55%). In that last group, almost one customer in two does not come back from one period to the next.

These figures date from 2018. They do not describe today's situation to the point, but they show a stable hierarchy between industries: where commitment is contractual or long-term, customers stay; where purchases are occasional, they move around.

The industries that talk to customers most retain the least

The paradox is striking. Hospitality, restaurants and retail are the industries with the most customer contact: stays, meals, checkouts, counter conversations, online reviews, questions before a purchase, complaints after it.

By contrast, an insurance or consulting client interacts rarely but is tied in by a contract. Conversation volume does not guarantee loyalty. It only guarantees that there is a large written and spoken record of what customers experience.

That is exactly where the opportunity lies for the industries at the bottom of the ranking: they have plenty of material to understand why their customers do not come back.

These customers speak up before they leave

A disappointed hotel guest almost never leaves in silence. They mention it at the front desk, write it in a review, or bring it up in an email after their stay. An online shopper contacts customer service about a late delivery, a wrong item or a slow refund.

The problem is not a lack of information. It is that the information is scattered: hundreds of reviews across several platforms, tickets in one tool, calls nobody listens to again. Reading all of it by hand is impossible beyond a few dozen messages a week.

As a result, teams react to the most visible cases and miss the recurring patterns, the ones that actually explain part of the customers leaving.

Online reviews make this especially visible. A guest who writes three sentences about a noisy room, a slow check-in and an unhelpful answer from staff is giving the hotel a precise list of what to fix. Multiply that by hundreds of reviews per property and per month, and the picture becomes very detailed.

What automatic language analysis changes

Automatic language analysis makes it possible to read every message, not just a sample. It picks up the emotions customers express, groups recurring topics, and tells a mildly annoyed customer apart from one who is considering not coming back.

For a hotel group, that means knowing whether cleanliness, noise, welcome or breakfast weighs most in negative reviews, property by property. For a retailer, it means spotting the delivery issues that cause the most frustration before they turn into customer loss.

Teams in these industries can see concrete examples on our hospitality and restaurants page.

How to act now

Three simple steps are enough to start. First, gather the sources you already have: online reviews, tickets, emails, call transcripts. Next, measure the share of negative messages and the topics that trigger them. Finally, track these indicators over time, alongside your retention rate.

The goal is not to replace classic indicators but to explain them. A retention rate tells you how many customers leave. Customers' own words tell you why, and often early enough to act.

Start small if needed: one property, one store or one product line over a quarter. The patterns that emerge are usually clear enough to justify extending the approach to the whole business.
